name: Thailand

income_tax.summary: Residents (180 days or more in a calendar year) pay progressive tax from 0% to 35% on net income; employment income gets a 50% expense deduction capped at THB 100,000 plus a THB 60,000 personal allowance. Foreign income earned from 2024 is taxable when remitted to Thailand. Employees pay 5% social security on wages up to THB 17,500 a month (max THB 875).
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Section 33 applies to employees (foreign employees with work permits included). Independent contractors without a Thai employer pay no mandatory contribution; whether foreigners may join voluntary Section 40 was not verified from an official SSO page. Self-employed (section 40(2) etc.) may deduct actual expenses or a standard 10-60% depending on the business; the exact rate per activity was not listed on the PwC page.
income_tax.local_tax_note: No local income tax. Bracket thresholds are on net income after the 50% employment expense deduction (max THB 100,000) and allowances (THB 60,000 taxpayer, THB 60,000 non-filing spouse). The social security cap is THB 17,500 x 12 = THB 210,000 of wages.

regimes.name: Long-Term Resident (LTR) visa - Highly-Skilled Professional
regimes.description: BOI Long-Term Resident visa for highly skilled professionals working in a targeted industry. The Revenue Department's LTR tax presentation states the 17% rate is a flat withholding rate on employment income, granted to Highly-Skilled Professionals (LTR-H) who work for a company operating in a targeted industry (as defined under the Competitiveness Enhancement for Target Industries Act, the Investment Promotion Act or the Eastern Economic Corridor Act). Conditions: the employer must notify the Area Revenue Office on the prescribed form and the 17% applies from the date the office acknowledges it; tax withheld at 17% can be treated as final, provided the holder does not claim a refund or credit; the holder still files PND 95 and needs a Tax ID. The separate exemption for foreign-sourced income belongs to the Wealthy Global Citizen, Wealthy Pensioner and Work-from-Thailand Professional categories, not to LTR-H.
regimes.duration_note: First permission 5 years, extendable by another 5 if still qualified. USD 80,000 a year average over the past two years; USD 40,000-80,000 needs extra proof (e.g. a master's degree in science or technology). Needs health insurance of USD 50,000 or Thai social security or USD 100,000 on deposit for 12 months. Fee THB 50,000.

sources.title: Tax Essentials for LTR Visa Holders (Revenue Department presentation)

open_questions: The Revenue Department slides do not state a cap or minimum for income taxed at 17%; whether it covers bonuses and benefits in kind was not checked.

regimes.name: Destination Thailand Visa (DTV)
regimes.description: Five-year multiple-entry visa with stays of up to 180 days each (extendable) and a THB 500,000 funds requirement per the e-visa site. It does not change tax: a holder staying 180 days or more in a year is a Thai tax resident, taxed on foreign income earned from 2024 only when remitted to Thailand.
regimes.duration_note: Five-year validity, 180 days per stay with an extension option. THB 500,000 in funds. Income test not given on the opened page.

residence_routes: EU, US and other citizens: the Destination Thailand Visa (DTV, five years, 180-day stays, THB 500,000 funds) suits remote workers; highly skilled employees can apply for the BOI Long-Term Resident visa (Highly-Skilled Professional: USD 80,000 average income, five years, extendable by five) or take a work visa and permit through a Thai employer. Visa-exempt entry does not allow work. Nationality does not change the routes, though visa-exemption and e-visa details vary by passport.
open_questions: 2-bedroom rent is a weak estimate (agency blog range midpoint).

Work-from-Thailand Professional LTR category (USD 80,000 income, foreign-sourced income exempt per the Revenue Department) is not modelled; whether its exemption reaches pay for work done in Thailand was not established.
